entry.title: A full class batch verified, including a float returned on the x87 stack
entry.summary: A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.
entry.content:
A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.

What was asked

Rewrite 42 related animation-channel methods in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original, with 1,000 trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All 42 methods passed 1,000 trials each with every wrong version caught; none were deferred.

Verified A Rust rewrite declared to return f32 leaves the value in the x87 ST0 register on this target, and the checker's x87 state comparison verifies it bit for bit, including signed zeros and quiet not-a-numbers. The brief lists x87 returns as not provable; that holds for doubles, but a single-precision x87 return works with no return channel compared and the x87 state check on.

Verified Indirect calls cannot be site-patched (the driver refuses anything that is not a direct call). They are intercepted by planting a stub address in the fabricated object table and having the rewrite load and call through it exactly like the original.

Verified Three separate copy and serialize loops return a reloaded count, not the last value they moved: each loop ends by loading the count into the return register after the final element. Two first attempts returned the last element and failed; reading the last register write before the return, not the loop body, gives the right answer.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes with an x87 single-precision return should attempt it with an f32 rewrite signature instead of deferring. Lanes should check what value the return register holds after a loop rather than assuming it holds the last computed value. The indirect-call planting pattern is now demonstrated and reusable.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; each verdict records 1,000 passing trials and each wrong-version verdict records a failure on the x87, heap, call or return comparison as appropriate.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two first attempts misread the original: a decoder slot was assumed to carry the object pointer when address arithmetic showed it carries the bit cursor, and a thread-block accessor was dereferenced once too often. A build briefly failed because a finished run still held the rewrite library file; a retry seconds later succeeded. All were fixed and re-proven in the same session.

entry.title: A stuck tick stopped the lanes: how one slow step took down three agents
entry.summary: At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.
entry.content:
At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.

LinkWhat happenedStatus
A finished lane left work runningA production lane ended at 17:54 and reported that nothing of its own was still running. Seventeen copies of one of its helper scripts were, and stayed busy for 52 to 117 minutes, about four processor cores between them. The watchdog stops such leftovers only when they are two and a half hours old.Verified (process list, command lines, ages)
The five-minute tick slowed to a crawlThe tick's rewrite importer reads every lane's results, about 1,500 folders, and normally takes a minute. From 18:30 it ran for more than ten, reading about 120 files a second with the disk idle and no paging. After the leftovers were stopped the same step took 57 seconds.Timing verified; the leftovers as the cause is inferred from that before and after, not proven
The supervisor waits for the tickThe supervisor starts lanes and runs the tick itself, and runs as one background task with a two-hour limit. It is written to finish by itself after 112 minutes. It was inside the tick when the 112 minutes passed, was still there when the two hours passed, and was stopped at the limit.Verified (supervisor log, task record)
Lanes are the supervisor's childrenStopping the task stopped everything it had started: three lanes that were 30 to 45 minutes into their work, among them the audit of blind proofs and the first class-completion lane.Verified

What was lost and what was not

No results were lost: lanes keep their state in their own folders and write results as they go. About two lane-hours of model work were interrupted, and for seven minutes nothing was running. A fourth lane had finished four minutes earlier and is unaffected: it verified 26 of 27 tiny forwarding functions in 25 minutes, all of them deferred as untestable by the project's earliest lanes, because the checker of that day could not follow a jump out of a function.

Changes

  • Every step of the tick has a time limit. A step that overruns is stopped with its whole process tree, the tick says so, and the remaining steps run. The limits add up to under fourteen minutes.
  • The supervisor runs no tick in the last eight minutes of its window, and the window is 100 minutes, so the worst case ends before the task's limit.
  • The lane launcher recognises a lane that was cut off from outside (its log shows a launch, work, and no exit) and resumes it from its folder instead of starting it again. The three lanes were resumed this way.
  • The watchdog stops a lane's leftover processes five minutes after that lane's launcher has logged its exit, instead of after two and a half hours.

What it says more generally

A lane's own statement that it left nothing running is a claim, not a fact; the check has to be made from outside, soon after the lane ends. And a controller that does housekeeping in its own loop inherits every way the housekeeping can stall.

entry.title: The largest families are the emptiest: what went into the workspace from the first two lifts, and what did not
entry.summary: Two lanes have now lifted families of verified functions into generic, portable Rust: the leaderboard class (3,195 verified rewrites) and four more families (2,392). The coordinator reviewed both trees today and moved two crates into the workspace. Three families were left out, and the reason changes how lift targets are chosen.
entry.content:
Two lanes have now lifted families of verified functions into generic, portable Rust: the leaderboard class (3,195 verified rewrites) and four more families (2,392). The coordinator reviewed both trees today and moved two crates into the workspace. Three families were left out, and the reason changes how lift targets are chosen.

FamilyVerified functions behind itWhat the lifted code holdsDecision
Leaderboard class: six table lookups, a probe, a row collector3,195Eight generic functions with loops, comparisons and a result map each, and one descriptor per leaderboard. Behaviour.In the workspace as crates/lf-leaderboard. Verified: 13 host tests pass; the pipeline built and tested it on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Script native handlers2,162Four short forwarding functions and a table: per native its name, its hash where known, how many script words it forwards, which of them are booleans, and how the answer is returned. Data, and useful data: it is the script machine's interface to the engine.In the workspace as crates/lf-script-natives, described as a dispatch table and not as lifted behaviour. Verified: 6 host tests pass.
Timer callback registrations81One function that makes one call through a trait, and a table of a name and an index per member. Most names are fragments of addresses, because nobody has named the things being registered. Nothing else.Not brought in and not counted as lifted. Each original passes one address to a registrar; the address is the whole content, and the lifted form replaces it with an index that means nothing yet. These are tables waiting for names.
Asset slot registrations80
Stored ratio refreshes69

Why it happened

The coordinator's brief for the second lift said to take the largest groups of same-shaped functions, in order of size. A group is large when the compiler stamped out one tiny routine hundreds of times, and the routines stamped out most often are start-up registrations and forwarders. So choosing by member count selects for the functions with the least in them. The lane did what it was asked, well, and its report said plainly where each crate's owner was unknown. The count it produced, "5,587 verified functions covered by lifted code", was true by its own definition and overstated what a port gains by at least those 230.

What a better target looks like

A class whose every method is verified: it has behaviour, it has a boundary the game itself drew, and nothing is missing in the middle. A census by class name (the part of a function's name before the last scope separator) gives, today:

MeasureValueStatus
Game functions with a class-qualified nameAbout 9,800 of 37,413Verified (census script over the inventory, the naming lanes and the verified index)
Classes with four or more named methods, all verified21 classes, 127 functions, 16,600 bytes, outside the leaderboard family: three audio voice classes, several animation channel decoders, a streaming device, a few task classesVerified
Classes with 70% or more of their bytes verified but not all467 classes, missing 1,327 functions and 60,000 bytes between themVerified
What "all verified" leaves outMethods nobody has named yet are invisible to the census. A class counted as complete may have virtual functions that are still anonymous.Known limit

Decisions

  • Lift targets are classes verified in full, not the largest shape groups. The animation channel decoders are first: 14 related classes, 100 named methods, 55 verified.
  • Production lanes take functions in address order, so a class is finished only by accident. A new kind of lane takes the missing methods of named classes, with the verified methods of the same classes named as the place to start. The first one has 42 methods of the animation channel classes.
  • A lifted function counts as lifted only if behaviour is in it. A family whose members differ only in an address is recorded as a table, and reported separately.
  • Both crates say in their own documentation that the lane's differential run against the verified rewrites has not been repeated by the pipeline. The test crates are large generated files and are still to come.

Follow-up on the 144 withdrawn rewrites

The entry "Verified, and wrong" recorded 144 rewrites of the leaderboard row collector that compared a length unsigned. A re-run lane has re-proven all 144 with the signed comparison. Its contracts script sixteen answers for the length helper, ten of them negative or edge values, and bias the other scripted answers so that those lengths reach the comparison; the unsigned mistake, run as a wrong version, fails on every one of the 144. They are back in the verified count. The same lane found the blind spot next door in the other direction: a neighbouring function of the family compares a count unsigned, its contracts script counts from 0 to 16 only, and a rewrite that compared signed would pass. That family and the 253 row-collector rewrites that were right but had the same blind proof are queued for the same treatment. Correction to the earlier entry: it gave the number of signed members as 269; by the verified index it is 253 with the family's standard name, plus a dozen named differently.

To reproduce the census: group the game's functions by the class part of their names and compare each group with the verified index.

entry.title: Float operand order needs a branch, not a black box
entry.summary: A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.
entry.content:
A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite bit-identical to the original with the checker, including bit-exact floating-point results with matching NaN signs. Two were verified over 1200 trials each with mutants caught; the third was fully triaged and deferred for time with an executable plan.

What was found

  • Verified The compiler swaps the operands of scalar float add and multiply even when the values pass through black-box barriers and even across no-inline call boundaries. Both swaps were seen in disassembly of built rewrites. Order decides the sign of a NaN result, so a swapped build fails trials that pair two differently-signed NaNs in one operation.
  • Verified Order matters only when both operands are NaN: a single NaN forwards that NaN either way, and invalid cases yield the same default NaN either way. Both shipped rewrites therefore test the bit patterns first, forward the destination operand explicitly on both-NaN, and run a plain operation otherwise. Subtraction and comparisons need no branch.
  • Verified A build that had silently swapped an addition still passed small probes, purely because no trial paired two NaNs there. The lesson is that float contracts must include both-NaN pairs with opposing signs in the same operation, or a luck-dependent proof looks full.
  • Verified The contract lint check caught two wrong patch offsets before anything ran, exactly the failure mode it exists to stop.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both rewrites in this batch use the NaN-branch design; one was retrofitted from the opaque-call form and re-verified, because the opaque-call form is rebuild-fragile.
  • Recommended: amend the brief's float rule so black box stays (it stops constant folding) but the order pin is the NaN branch, and require opposing-sign NaN pairs in float input pools.
  • Previously verified float rewrites that rely on the black box alone are correct as built, but a toolchain change could silently swap them; re-running their contracts after such a change would catch it.

How to reproduce it

Build any rewrite whose float helpers are plain operations wrapped only in black boxes, disassemble the helper, and check which parameter ends up as the instruction destination; then run trials pairing plus-NaN with minus-NaN in one addition. The lane's report records the exact trial shape (a sum of three products over infinite and NaN inputs) and a pool layout that keeps the call path hot while carrying NaN coverage.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • For several builds the lane believed a memory source operand propagates NaN signs differently from a register source. That theory was wrong: re-examination found a swapped addition missed in an interleaved listing. It cost about twenty minutes and is recorded so nobody chases it again.
  • One rebuild failed on a locked output file because a worker from the previous run was still exiting; waiting for prior processes to clear before rebuilding fixed it.
  • The deferred function hides two quirks future lanes should know: two of its three multi-argument call shapes pass identical arguments and differ only in one register, and that register carries uninitialized frame fill (zero) in two shapes. Both were verified by hand-tracking the stack pointer and are in the lane report.

entry.title: Pin cycles in lockstep hide branch combinations
entry.summary: Verified A contract whose pinned inputs all cycle with the same period tests far fewer branch combinations than its author thinks: equal-length cycles march in lockstep, so some flag pairs never co-occur. Giving each pin a different cycle length took one function from four to ten call shapes with no other change.
entry.content:
Verified A contract whose pinned inputs all cycle with the same period tests far fewer branch combinations than its author thinks: equal-length cycles march in lockstep, so some flag pairs never co-occur. Giving each pin a different cycle length took one function from four to ten call shapes with no other change.

What was asked

Rewrite and verify a single large audio function with eleven scripted callees and about ten flag-driven branches.

What was found

Verified The first passing run covered only four call shapes. Three flag pins with two values each always agreed with the main enable flag, so whole combinations (a shaper call after the worker call, a path without the final helper) never ran, and both self-initialising parameter blocks only ever took their already-initialised path.

Verified A related gap: scripted callee outputs are consumed only on trials where that callee fires, so some script rows are dead and live rows can miss values the real callee produces. One row meant to drive a negative-index path never coincided with its callee firing.

Verified After giving pins cycle lengths of two, three, four, five and six, and placing script rows on live phases, the same rewrite passed with ten call shapes, every callee firing hundreds of times, and every parameter-block path taken.

What was decided or recommended

Pin cycles in a contract should use differing lengths so flag combinations mix across trials, and script rows for conditionally fired callees should be audited for which trial phases actually consume them. Both checks are cheap and static.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract with two or more equal-length pin cycles on branch flags, run it, and count distinct call shapes in the verdict coverage. Then change one cycle length and re-run: new shapes appear.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first deliberately wrong version of the rewrite passed all trials: the omitted store wrote back the value just read on some paths and was overwritten by a scripted callee output on the rest. It was replaced with a wrong version that omits a store nothing masks, which fails on the heap comparison as required.

entry.title: Two audio updates verified, and two disassembly traps
entry.summary: Both functions in this audio batch now have verified Rust rewrites, each proved identical to the original over 1200 trials, but the interesting part of the lane was the two mistakes in reading the original that the checker caught.
entry.content:
Both functions in this audio batch now have verified Rust rewrites, each proved identical to the original over 1200 trials, but the interesting part of the lane was the two mistakes in reading the original that the checker caught.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, including a deliberately wrong version per function that the proof must reject.

What was found

Verified Both rewrites passed all 1200 trials with bit-exact float comparison, all checks on, and each wrong version was rejected for the right reason.

Verified A pushed register before a call is an argument, not a save. One function pushes a register and then its actual argument before calling a filter; reading the first push as a register save understates the callee's arity by one, which shifts every later stack read by four bytes. The same filter is called elsewhere with two visible pushes and no caller cleanup, which proves it pops two words.

Verified A flag-capture followed by a test and a conditional jump tests the test, not the capture. The sequence captures the floating-point comparison flags into a byte register, masks that byte, and jumps on parity — but the masking instruction itself overwrites the flags first, so the jump observes the parity of the masked value. The result is equality against a constant, not the NaN check it resembles: only an exactly equal input takes one side.

Verified Speed-reading drops instructions. Three one-line register reloads were missed on the first pass, each of which changed a call argument or a branch on some path. A mechanical listing of every write to the register found all three at once.

What was decided or recommended

Count pushes against caller cleanup to fix callee arity, and cross-check the same callee at its other call sites before writing the contract. Audit every stack-slot read against the pushes outstanding at that exact point, and grep for register writes rather than trusting a first read.

How to reproduce it

Run the two contracts in the lane folder with the stock checker driver and worker; each passes 1200 trials with bit-exact floats, and each bundled wrong version fails. The contract generators, the per-trial diagnosis script, and the full report with evidence labels are in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

The parity-trap finding took the longest: the wrong mental model predicted one constant on a trial where the original wrote zero, and every theory about scripting or indexing failed until the flag flow was re-read instruction by instruction. The pushed-register finding went through a longer loop first, including a stretch suspecting the checker's stub code of clobbering a register it provably preserves, before the missed reloads explained everything.

entry.title: Cmpnless means greater-than
entry.summary: A large blend routine failed its proof on exact-integer loop counts only, because the disassembler's cmpnless mnemonic was transcribed as not-less-than when it is predicate 6, not-less-or-equal, a greater-than test.
entry.content:
A large blend routine failed its proof on exact-integer loop counts only, because the disassembler's cmpnless mnemonic was transcribed as not-less-than when it is predicate 6, not-less-or-equal, a greater-than test.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring routines of one animation subsystem in Rust and prove each identical to the original over a thousand trials.

What was found

Verified All four routines verified with bit-exact floating point results and a caught wrong version each; the largest is proven on its main path with the remaining paths specified as a retry kit.

Verified The blend routine counts loop iterations with a round-and-fixup idiom whose final test disassembles as cmpnless. That mnemonic is comparison predicate 6, which is true when the first operand is greater than the second, not when it is not less than it. The two readings differ only when both operands are equal, so every fractional quotient rounded correctly and only exact integers miscounted: the original ran three iterations where the rewrite ran two. A probe contract that added exactly one to an output per iteration measured both counts directly and confirmed the one-line fix.

Inferred The checker's call stand-in zeroes the upper words of one vector register on the original side between two neighbouring helper calls. Only unlogged registers are affected, so no verdict is at risk, but one helper's vector argument had to stay uncompared because of it.

What was decided or recommended

Transcribe cmpnless as greater-than everywhere; audit other rewrites that read it as not-less-than, since the bug hides on all non-integer inputs. Anyone extending the blend proof should start from the retry kit in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

Pin the routine's two vector inputs and the limit it reads from its object so the quotient is an exact integer, stub the helpers with fixed rows, and compare iteration counts; or read predicate 6 in the processor manual's compare-pages.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first mismatch looked like a broken formula: every output word differed. Pinning each path separately showed the tail and the loop-free paths passing, which isolated the loop; only then did a counting probe reveal a miscount rather than a miscomputation. Two earlier hypotheses, relocated float constants and mismatched stub rows, were each disproven by a direct check before the instruction reading was questioned.

entry.title: Lifting the next families: script natives and three more
entry.summary: Four tiny routines now cover 2,392 verified functions: nearly every script native handler is one dispatch routine in four return conventions, and the timer, asset-slot and ratio-refresh groups are one routine each. Every member is proven against its verified rewrite by differential test.
entry.content:
Four tiny routines now cover 2,392 verified functions: nearly every script native handler is one dispatch routine in four return conventions, and the timer, asset-slot and ratio-refresh groups are one routine each. Every member is proven against its verified rewrite by differential test.

What was asked

Repeat the leaderboard lift on the next largest families of verified functions: script native handlers in several shapes, timer register callbacks, asset slot getters and refresh ratio writers, taking them one proven group at a time.

What was found

Verified The native handlers are far more uniform than their count suggests. Of 2,620 verified handlers, 2,162 are one engine call forwarding sequential script words, with per-word boolean coercion and four return conventions: return the answer, store its low byte, store the whole word, or return zero. What varies per handler is only its dispatch entry: name, hash, word count and coercion flags.

Verified The other three groups are each exactly one routine: timer callbacks pass one address to a registrar, asset slots pass a slot record and a name to a registry routine, and ratio refreshers divide two stored floats into a third. All 80 asset names were read back from the executable and match.

Verified The census corrected two labels from the earlier survey: the second native group forwards two arguments with no return, and most timer-group members carry other names. Operand-level checking also surfaced real variants the structural hash had merged: boolean coercions, a stack-slot quirk word, float-answering engine calls, and zero returns.

FamilyMembers proven
Native dispatch, four conventions2,162
Timer registrations81
Asset registrations80
Ratio refreshes69

What was decided or recommended

  • Natives go to the script subsystem, timer registrations to the main loop; asset slots probably belong to streaming and the ratio bank's owner is still unknown, so it keeps its own crate for now.
  • 458 natives are deferred with stated reasons: bespoke argument plumbing, global-gated handlers that need their subsystem state first, float-computing handlers that form their own group, and spellings that need their lane's context layout.
  • Next groups in order: model registrations, timer initialisers, vehicle ratios, leaderboard constructors, and cache lookups.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's census and generator scripts over the verified rewrites to rebuild the descriptor tables and differential cases, then run the seven differential suites on the 32-bit target and the four crates' own tests on the 64-bit host. Every case also runs a deliberately wrong lift that must be caught. Together with the leaderboard family, 5,587 verified rewrites are now covered by lifted code.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Three defects were found by the proof rather than by reading: engine calls declared with float answers read a different return register than integer stubs provide, so those cases needed float-answering stubs; a residue spelling in store returns needed pinning per member instead of assuming two spellings; and parallel test suites shared one relocated base until each suite took it inside its own session. Each fix was confirmed by the full suite going green.

entry.title: Verified, and wrong: 144 rewrites that the checker passed and the lift caught
entry.summary: The first lift at scale turned one template family, the leaderboard class, into a handful of generic functions written from the original, and proved them by running every verified rewrite of the family against them. That cross-check found something the checker had not: 144 verified rewrites of one function differ from the original. They have been withdrawn from the verified count. This entry records what happened, because it says something about what "verified" has meant so far.
entry.content:
The first lift at scale turned one template family, the leaderboard class, into a handful of generic functions written from the original, and proved them by running every verified rewrite of the family against them. That cross-check found something the checker had not: 144 verified rewrites of one function differ from the original. They have been withdrawn from the verified count. This entry records what happened, because it says something about what "verified" has meant so far.

FactValueStatus
FunctionThe family's row collector: one routine, instantiated once per leaderboard, 413 instantiations verified at the time.Verified
The differenceInside its loop the function asks a helper for a row's length and compares it with eight. The original compares it as a signed number: a negative length counts as small and the row is copied. 144 rewrites compare it unsigned: a negative length counts as huge and the row is not copied. The other 269 compare it signed.Verified twice: the lift's harness runs each of the 144 with such lengths and shows the difference, and in 60 of 60 originals read independently the compare is followed by the signed jump
Why the checker passed themThe length comes from a callee, and a callee is replaced by a stand-in whose answers the contract scripts. No contract ever scripted a negative answer. Every trial ran, every comparison matched, and the one input class that separates the two versions was never tried.Verified (read from contracts of both groups)
Why the wrong-version test did not helpEach function had its own deliberately wrong version, and each was caught. But the lanes chose wrong versions such as a query id off by one. A wrong version shows that the contract can see that one change; it says nothing about a change nobody thought to make.Verified
How two groups aroseEighteen lanes verified members of this family, eight at a time, each working the routine out again. Some read the jump correctly and some did not. A single generator lane later did 117 members from one template, all signed.Verified (lanes named in the index)

What this says about the count

The checker proves that two pieces of code agree on the inputs it was given. For values the function receives directly, the inputs are generated with edge cases. For values that come back from callees, the inputs are whatever the lane scripted, and lanes script small values that steer the function down its paths. So any comparison made on a callee's answer has been tested only as far as the lane thought to test it. This family made the gap visible because the same routine was rewritten many times by different lanes and then compared. For a function rewritten once, nothing would have shown it. How many verified functions share this blind spot is not known; it is now a question with an audit attached, not an assumption.

Decisions

  • The 144 are removed from the verified tree, and the published count went down by 144 for this reason. They return only through a re-run lane whose contracts make the length helper answer with negative and edge values, and whose wrong version is exactly this mistake.
  • The 269 rewrites that compare correctly keep their place, with a note that their proofs are blind on the same point and are to be strengthened the same way.
  • The production brief (version b17) now requires, for every comparison made on a callee's answer, scripted answers that separate signed from unsigned and an exact bound from one off by one, and a wrong version that makes exactly that mistake.
  • An audit is to measure the blind spot across the verified tree: flip the signedness of comparisons on callee results in a sample of verified rewrites and count how many of those wrong versions pass their existing contracts.
  • The lift is now also a check. Wherever many verified rewrites share one routine, lifting them compares them with one another and with a version written from the original, at almost no cost.

To reproduce: take the verified rewrites of one template function, run each against one reference version on inputs that include negative answers from the length helper, and group them by result.

entry.title: A rebuild routine that returns with a scratch register holding float bits
entry.summary: Verified One combiner-request rebuild routine in the motion timing tree returns to its caller with a callee-saved register holding the bit pattern of a single-precision float instead of the value it entered with.
entry.content:
Verified One combiner-request rebuild routine in the motion timing tree returns to its caller with a callee-saved register holding the bit pattern of a single-precision float instead of the value it entered with.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty small timing-tree routines in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified The rebuild routine passes a float to one of its callees twice: once in a vector register, where the callee actually reads it, and once by storing it over the stack slot that holds the routine's own saved register. The callee consumes that slot as its stack word, so when the routine later restores the register it loads the float bits instead. The function still works, because nothing reads the restored value afterwards, but the register violation is real: any caller keeping that register live across the call would be corrupted.

Verified The checker does not compare callee-saved registers, so the quirk is invisible to the proof. The rewrite preserves the register normally and matches on everything the checker observes: one thousand trials with no failures, plus a deliberately wrong version that was caught.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite was accepted as verified. If the checker ever gains a callee-saved-register comparison, this routine will need an exemption or a wider contract, because no safe Rust rewrite can reproduce the trashed register. Lanes meeting a similar spill-over-save-slot shape should check the epilogue register values before assuming the routine preserves them.

How to reproduce it

Read the rebuild routine's bytes through the mapped executable image and follow the stack pointer: three registers are saved on entry, the float is stored to the top stack slot, the indirect call that follows pops exactly that slot, and the matching restore at the end therefore loads the float. The checker's stack-pointer check passes throughout, which confirms the call cleans exactly one word.

What was confusing or went wrong

The cleanup shape of the float-receiving call was settled only on the third attempt. A pop-nothing model made the later argument reads land on the wrong words, and a pop-one-word model broke the stack balance; exact bookkeeping of pushed bytes against the return instruction's pop count showed the callee must leave the stack exactly as it found it apart from its return address. Two argument positions in the same routine were also misread on the first attempt by counting live pushes wrong; the checker's call log showed the swap immediately.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: trains, intermezzo cameras and the slot-inheritance trick
entry.summary: 147 of 150 consecutive functions got descriptive names. The batch turned out to be five groups, not one: vehicle physics and navigation helpers, the train system, the intermezzo cutscene-camera system with nine event classes, two intro-data loaders, and the final camera.
entry.content:
147 of 150 consecutive functions got descriptive names. The batch turned out to be five groups, not one: vehicle physics and navigation helpers, the train system, the intermezzo cutscene-camera system with nine event classes, two intro-data loaders, and the final camera.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, with a confidence grade, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from the strongest available evidence.

What was found

Verified The most reliable naming signal was slot inheritance: when a function overrides a virtual-table slot whose sibling override is already named, and it calls or tail-jumps to that sibling or base, it is the same method. This named most train, automobile and camera slots.

Verified Matching already-named functions to virtual-table slots by target address recovered the method layout of two class families: the general camera slots for attach, update, publish and deactivate, and the seven-step event lifecycle of start, update, stop, two condition checks, a start check and a name getter.

Verified The intermezzo camera builds all nine of its event objects inline in one construction routine, and picks the active event through a small start routine that runs the event's own start method and then its start check.

Inferred The navigation helpers form a small subsystem of their own: a periodic tick-gated update driving a table pass, a cell-grid build and a box-tree query, plus a point registry with snapshot support.

What was decided or recommended

Three functions were left unnamed with low confidence: a single flag-byte setter, a car-or-tail-car word reader, and one entry that lands in the middle of the intro-spline loader rather than at a function start. A later lane should not name that address without fixing the split. The event-lifecycle wording (start, stop, condition checks) is mine and should be checked against the callers of neighbouring batches before it hardens into convention.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: every direct-call target resolved against the merged names, the lane names and the verified index, plus referenced strings and float-operation counts. Then match named siblings to virtual-table slots to get the slot map, read the short functions fully, and confirm each override by its call or tail jump to the base. A caller map from a single executable-section scan resolved several otherwise ambiguous helpers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two inherited names were traps. A function named as a leaderboard getter turned out to be a constant stub returning a fixed number, called from camera code for that constant. A frequent shared callee turned out to be a stack-probing helper with no semantic meaning. Both are now noted so later lanes do not build theories on them. Several train-prefixed names from an earlier lane cover generic physics code that replay-camera code also calls.

entry.title: Production batch: four animation functions verified, one truncated inventory entry, one rotation quirk
entry.summary: Four animation-system functions were rewritten in Rust and each passed one thousand differential trials against the original with its deliberately wrong version caught, including a large twelve-call compressor verified through eight scripted callee stand-ins.
entry.content:
Four animation-system functions were rewritten in Rust and each passed one thousand differential trials against the original with its deliberately wrong version caught, including a large twelve-call compressor verified through eight scripted callee stand-ins.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of four original game functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the stock checker, one thousand trials each, with a wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All four rewrites passed one thousand trials with zero failures and full original-side completion; every wrong version failed as required.

FunctionSizeResult
Mover pose refreshmedium, two callsverified, second attempt
Bitset buildersmall, allocator callverified, second attempt
Delta channel compressorlarge, twelve callsverified, second attempt
Quantized samplersmall, three callsverified, first attempt

Verified The function inventory lists the large compressor as nineteen bytes shorter than it really is: a listing cut at the listed size ends in the middle of its epilogue. Decoding past the listed end reaches a normal return.

Verified The bitset builder sets each inner-loop bit one position ahead of its index, wrapping inside the machine word at word ends instead of advancing to the next word. The rewrite reproduces this exactly. Inferred It reads like an off-by-one in the original, but it may be intentional.

What was decided or recommended

  • Re-derive the truncated inventory entry and scan for other entries whose bytes do not end at a return or terminal jump.
  • Keep the rotation quirk as reproduced behavior, flagged as a suspected original bug, until someone with engine context confirms intent.

How to reproduce it

Run each of the four proof contracts in the lane scratch folder with the stock checker driver and worker: one thousand trials each, then each recorded wrong version, which must fail. The large function needs its generator script, which asserts the trial alignment of its eight scripted callee cycles before emitting the contract.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two first attempts failed on frame-address arithmetic after pushed arguments shifted the stack: in both cases values first read as dead turned out to be live outputs. One failure needed the full call log, but mismatch reports print only the first three calls, so a display-only full log dump was added to the lane's driver copy; the verdicts themselves come from unmodified comparison logic.

entry.title: Lifting one template family: three thousand verified functions into a handful
entry.summary: The first lift at scale worked: the largest template family in the game, the per-leaderboard info class with over three thousand verified rewrites, is now eight generic functions plus a generated table of per-leaderboard parameters, proven against every one of the original rewrites by differential test.
entry.content:
The first lift at scale worked: the largest template family in the game, the per-leaderboard info class with over three thousand verified rewrites, is now eight generic functions plus a generated table of per-leaderboard parameters, proven against every one of the original rewrites by differential test.

What was asked

Take the project's largest template family, one class template instantiated once per leaderboard with eight virtual functions per instantiation, and lift it to portable Rust: one generic function per virtual slot, parameters from a descriptor table, collaborators through traits, no addresses, no unsafe. Prove each slot against the verified 32-bit rewrites with differential tests, and measure what the lift takes.

What was found

Verified Each of the eight slots has exactly one shape; instantiations differ only in board constants, callee identities, and, for the row-processing slot, the row count and one comparison detail. All 3,195 slot rewrites are covered by differential tests and all pass, on the 32-bit target and on the 64-bit host.

Verified The lift is about 1,100 lines of safe Rust against 175,000 lines of 32-bit rewrite code, with zero unsafe in the lifted crate. Three narrowings in the proof are stated openly: one group of rewrites uses an unsigned comparison where the original uses a signed one, so the lift follows the original and the proof is scoped to the domain where they agree; a small group of whole-register returns is compared on the low byte only; and one slot's raw output pointer is narrowed to an optional handle with the pointer shape pinned by a separate test.

Verified Clustering all other verified rewrites by structural shape shows the next targets: script-native wrappers share a handful of tiny routines hundreds of times each, and three smaller families (timer callbacks, asset slots, refresh writers) repeat one routine each dozens of times.

What was decided or recommended

Lift the script natives next with the same census, descriptor table, and differential proof pipeline; then the three smaller families. Constructors of this family are designed but not lifted and are the natural follow-up. Where the original and a verified rewrite disagree, the lift follows the original and says so.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's census and generator scripts over the verified rewrites to rebuild the descriptor table and the differential tests, then run the lift crate's tests on the host and the differential suite on the 32-bit target. Generation asserts each member's shape, so drift in the rewrite set fails loudly rather than silently.

What was confusing or went wrong

The rewrite index grew twice mid-lane as other lanes committed, so every count moved and all generators were rerun from scripts rather than patched by hand. Twenty-four files first assumed to be constructors turned out, by shape and by passing proof, to be misnamed members of the tag-fetch slot. A fabricated test double for one slot's collaborator silently read the wrong fields until a dedicated regression test pinned the layout.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed because the global-write log drops word addresses
entry.summary: Verified The checker's comparison of written globals ignores which word inside a declared range each value was written to, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. A rewrite with one four-word block at the wrong slot offset passed 1188 of 1200 trials.
entry.content:
Verified The checker's comparison of written globals ignores which word inside a declared range each value was written to, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. A rewrite with one four-word block at the wrong slot offset passed 1188 of 1200 trials.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring functions (a large effect-slot allocator and a small vector routine) and prove each identical to the original with the checker.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified: 1200 trials each, zero failures, non-vacuous, deliberately wrong versions caught for both.

Verified While debugging the large function, its contract declared the whole slot table as one watched range. The worker records every changed word in a range as the range base plus the value, so the verdict compared only the sequence of values, not their addresses. A rewrite that copied one block 96 bytes too low produced the same value sequence on trials where nothing else was written between the two addresses, and passed.

Verified Declaring the table as one single-word range per word restored exact addresses and the same rewrite failed immediately with the true offsets visible. The final contract keeps that shape (679 one-word ranges); no checker code was changed for any verdict.

What was decided or recommended

Record the word address, not the range base, in the globals-write log. Until that lands, contracts covering a table with a single wide range should split it into small ranges so misplaced stores cannot hide. Past verdicts over wide ranges were weaker than they looked wherever a rewrite could shift a block without changing the value order.

How to reproduce it

Declare one multi-word globals range, run a rewrite that writes the range's expected values shifted by one word with nothing interleaved, and observe a pass. Then split the range into one-word ranges and observe the failure with exact addresses.

What was confusing or went wrong

The passing-but-wrong rewrite cost two debug cycles: the value-only log made the misplaced block invisible, and only trials where unrelated writes interleaved between the true and wrong addresses failed, which first looked like a different bug. A second wrong assumption (which helper answer a store used) hid behind the same weak comparison until the ranges were split.

entry.title: Two coverage traps in a 3,394-byte ped-task function
entry.summary: A single-function production lane verified one of the largest functions attempted so far, a ped task refresh routine of about eight hundred instructions and ninety call sites, in twelve hundred trials with zero failures. The rewrite itself was straightforward; nearly all of the debugging time went to two contract traps that other lanes will hit, both found the hard way.
entry.content:
A single-function production lane verified one of the largest functions attempted so far, a ped task refresh routine of about eight hundred instructions and ninety call sites, in twelve hundred trials with zero failures. The rewrite itself was straightforward; nearly all of the debugging time went to two contract traps that other lanes will hit, both found the hard way.

What was asked

Rewrite the function in Rust and prove the rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version five checker, covering every outgoing call and every reachable branch.

What was found

Verified First, the register comparison list is opt-out for method calls, not opt-in. The lane-facing manual describes the list as optional, but the worker compares the object register by default for every method-style callee. Any callee whose register holds a stack address or a leftover value therefore fails until it is explicitly listed with an empty set. Four callees in this function needed that treatment.

Verified Second, fabrication cycles with the same length are phase-locked. Every two-valued null-or-object pin in the first contract was null on exactly the same trials, which made gate-plus-creation combinations structurally impossible and left fifteen callees unfired no matter how many trials ran. The fix was mixed cycle lengths with hand-checked phases so every required combination actually occurs in the trial window.

Verified A supporting check also proved its worth: a stack-depth dataflow over the whole function, using each callee's cleanup behavior from its own epilogue, closed with zero conflicts at every control-flow join, which validated all thirty-five call signatures at once before the first run.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes should explicitly decide the register list for every method-style callee, including an empty list with a reason, rather than leaving it out. Lanes with several nullable inputs should use mixed cycle lengths and verify by hand that each required combination of values occurs at some trial number, instead of assuming more trials will cover it.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contract generator and checker contract for the batch function with twelve hundred trials, then repeat with a second seed; both pass with zero failures and full callee coverage. The deliberately wrong version, which flips one bit of a heap word the original always writes, fails on the heap check as required.

What was confusing or went wrong

The empty-register-list fix was initially misread as the cause of an unrelated failure, because the mismatch display truncates call details to a shared prefix; full per-call logs from a temporary debug print in the lane's own driver copy showed the real divergence. The phase-lock problem survived one full passing run, since the unfired callees only showed up as a vacuous verdict, not a failure.

entry.title: A production batch that caught the manual out
entry.summary: Three task functions were rewritten and verified, and the checker manual turned out to name the wrong key for the return channel.
entry.content:
Three task functions were rewritten and verified, and the checker manual turned out to name the wrong key for the return channel.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring task functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original through the project's checker, with a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All three rewrites passed one thousand trials each with no failures and no vacuous verdicts, and all three wrong versions were caught.

Verified The manual says the contract's top level return key selects what is compared, but the worker reads the key inside the checks block instead. With only the top level key set, full register contents were compared and dozens of correct trials failed on leftover high bytes. Setting both keys fixed it. The failure mode is fail-closed, but the manual misleads.

Verified The worker's stack comparison does not see scratch writes to the incoming argument slot or below the stack pointer, so functions using those tricks keep the full stack check with no narrowing.

Verified A vehicle data table the code reads is entirely zeros in the untouched executable and is filled in at start-up. Seeding it per trial through the checker's global fills tests the true path; without seeding those trials fault identically on both sides.

What was decided or recommended

  • Set the return channel in both places until the manual is fixed.
  • Seed runtime-filled tables through global fills rather than leaving those branches to fault parity.
  • Show the first diverging call in mismatch reports, not just the first three calls.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch contracts with the stock checker and compare the verdicts with the return key set in one place versus both. Read the named table's entries from the executable image to confirm they are zeros.

What was confusing or went wrong

The checker's verdict detail shows only the first three calls, which looked identical on both sides while the verdict failed; the real divergence was at a later call. A reporting-only addition to a private driver copy exposed it. The driver also overwrote the lane's own results file once; later runs used a separate output folder.

entry.title: An outside review of the pipeline, checked against the machine: five findings, six changes
entry.summary: An outside reader went through the public changelog and argued that the next gains were in the pipeline, not in making lanes write code faster: the memory ceiling, routing work by what the checker can do, the publication scan as a hidden tax, deferrals as queues, and measuring by bytes instead of functions. Each point was checked against the machine before anything was built. Most held, two were larger than the reader could have known, and one led somewhere else.
entry.content:
An outside reader went through the public changelog and argued that the next gains were in the pipeline, not in making lanes write code faster: the memory ceiling, routing work by what the checker can do, the publication scan as a hidden tax, deferrals as queues, and measuring by bytes instead of functions. Each point was checked against the machine before anything was built. Most held, two were larger than the reader could have known, and one led somewhere else.

PointWhat the machine showedStatus
Memory ceilingThe kernel's non-paged pool is at 15.7 GB and still growing; about 20 lanes fit of a target of 52. A census of every open handle found one platform service from the chip vendor holding 81,215 thread handles, 84% of all thread handles on the machine, up from 68,740 eight hours earlier. A thread that has ended stays in kernel memory while a handle to it is open, and so does its process. Over those eight hours the pool grew by about 96 KB per handle that service gained.Handle counts Verified. That the service is the cause is Inferred from the correlation; kernel pool tags cannot be read without administrator rights.
Publication scan as a taxWorse than reported: 737 verified rewrites (131,000 bytes) were sitting in lane folders, out of the repository and out of the verified count. The scan's pattern had no word boundary after a register name, so "test always" and "call chain" read as assembly; and most of the rest were comments noting a calling convention by quoting the return instruction. Only 17 had a match in code.Verified
Route by checker abilityDisassembling all 38,194 game functions takes 14 seconds. 989 functions holding 932,000 bytes very probably pass a double across a call in a vector register, which the installed checker cannot carry: far more than the handful of deferrals had suggested. The scan flags the functions a lane had spent an hour on that morning. Separately, the batch maker's eligibility rule was still the one written for the second version of the checker and was keeping about 1,600 functions out of the queue for abilities added since.Verified (counts); the double label is a heuristic and over-counts somewhat
Deferrals as queues1,046 functions holding 678,000 bytes are deferred and not since verified. Sorted by what would clear them: proven only in stages (64 functions, 181,000 bytes), deferred for lack of lane time (482, 137,000), an indirect call the lane could not route (132, 114,000), doubles in vector registers (95, 108,000), and smaller ones.Verified
Measure by bytesAfter the held rewrites came in: 39% of functions verified but 25.4% of the code by size. Functions of 1,000 bytes and more hold 38% of the game's code and 14.6% of that is verified.Verified
Stalls should raise alarmsTrue, and it had already cost an hour of small-function lanes.Verified

What was changed

  • The scan's pattern now requires a real register or operand, and the importer rewords comments that quote an instruction or bytes of the original. The sanitizer touches comment text only and checks that itself: the text with comments removed must be identical before and after. 715 rewrites entered the repository on the next tick; the verified count rose by that many for this reason and no other.
  • A preflight table records, for every function, what it will ask of the checker. The batch maker holds a function out while it needs an ability the checker lacks, admits the ones the old rule excluded, and writes each function's labels into the batch list so a lane knows at triage.
  • Deferred functions are grouped into queues with the action that clears each, and a new lane kind takes a batch from the largest actionable queue, one lane slot in twelve.
  • Another new lane kind takes only functions of 1,500 bytes and more, two slots in twelve, to find early what the largest functions need.
  • A lane kind that produces no lane while its queue is not empty now raises an alarm that the five-minute status shows.
  • The published progress data carries the share of code verified by size and the share in large functions.

What was not built, and why

  • A scheduler that scores every piece of work by expected bytes, success probability and cost. The measurements it needs now exist (bytes per lane-hour by kind, the queues, the preflight labels); the lane mix is set from them by hand each hour. Automating that choice comes after the labels have a day of data behind them.
  • A shared checker service. Lanes' checker workers are a small part of memory (about 100 MB each, only while a run is in progress); the ceiling is the kernel, not the workers.
  • Leases with checkpoints. A lane's results file and batch list already are its checkpoint; a lane cut off by the service is resumed twice, and whatever an ended lane did not settle goes back to the queue.

What is still the owner's decision

Restarting the vendor's service (or the machine) to release the handles. It is a system service, it needs administrator rights, and the coordinator does not touch it.

To reproduce the handle census: ask the system for every open handle with the object type of each, group by owning process, and look for a process whose thread handles outnumber the machine's live threads many times over.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch through vtable slots and twin diffs
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering rain effects, vehicle audio and vehicle code yielded eighty-four names, with vtable slot joins doing most of the work.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering rain effects, vehicle audio and vehicle code yielded eighty-four names, with vtable slot joins doing most of the work.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed functions, with a confidence per name, working from strings, callers, callees and class information rather than reading every function.

What was found

Verified The run splits into rain particle effects code, boat audio code, a materials data loader, train and cable car audio code, radio emitter slots and vehicle class slots, plus thirty-three labels that are not functions.

Verified Dumping the vehicle and audio vtables from the binary and joining slot numbers with already-named sibling overrides named most vehicle slots, including shared base-class implementations used by several classes at once.

Verified Two pairs of near-identical neighbours differ only in where they take an entity from, so one variant serves an external tick and the other an in-update call.

Verified About a fifth of the batch are size-zero inventory labels pointing at mid-function code, jump targets or epilogues; one listed size swallowed four following functions.

What was decided or recommended

Later naming lanes should join vtable slots against prior lane names first, diff near-identical neighbours before reading them, and verify inventory sizes against the first return instruction.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image, build one evidence table of strings, calls and callers for the whole batch, dump the relevant class vtables and match slot numbers to named siblings, then disassemble only the short and unclear functions fully.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three functions funnel into encrypted code so their behaviour stays hidden, and a family of handling float-math helpers was left unnamed because the exact outputs could not be pinned down. Nearest-name caller matches beyond a few dozen bytes proved unreliable and were used only as supporting hints.

entry.title: A dead scan loop and a vector-register gap on the peds-tasks batch
entry.summary: Three of five task-system functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over a thousand trials each; the other two were deferred with precise missing checker abilities, and one verified function turned out to contain a scan loop that can never find anything.
entry.content:
Three of five task-system functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over a thousand trials each; the other two were deferred with precise missing checker abilities, and one verified function turned out to contain a scan loop that can never find anything.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original through the project's checker, with a deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified Three functions passed a thousand trials each with exact float matches and full branch coverage, and every wrong version was caught.

Verified One function's ten-slot result scan is dead code in the original: the slots are zeroed by the function's own stores and no callee receives a pointer to them, so the two inner probe calls can never run. They stay declared and intercepted but exempt from coverage.

Verified One function passes double-precision arguments in vector registers, which the checker cannot transport: the rewrite side moves one word per register while the comparison checks all four. Only all-zero doubles could match, so it was deferred rather than narrowed into a vacuous proof.

Verified One function's main loop is unreachable under call interception: the function zeroes its own loop count and only an intercepted callee could set it back, which stubs cannot do for absolute globals. Only the empty-table path runs, and that alone was not claimed as a proof.

What was decided or recommended

The three passing rewrites were recorded as verified with their narrowings stated. The two deferred functions each got a retry kit naming the exact missing ability: a two-word vector-register transport, and stub writes to absolute globals. A wrong frame-map computation that cost a full attempt is recorded as a caution to re-derive stack layouts from the push and store order.

How to reproduce it

Each verified function ships its contract and verdict files; rerunning the checker driver on any contract reproduces the thousand-trial proof and the wrong-version failure.

What was confusing or went wrong

A single stack-arithmetic slip placed a block of zero stores eighteen hex digits from its true location, which simultaneously misidentified the scan contents, the tail index, and the fill model. The probe failures contradicted the model on all three points at once, and re-deriving the frame map from the instruction order fixed all three together.

entry.title: Naming batch 110: replay cameras, planes, coronas, nav and portals
entry.summary: Verified A batch of 150 consecutive functions split cleanly into eight groups in address order: replay-camera helpers, a shared-memory media channel, particle sample baking, planes and ambient planes, corona light sprites, the nav and path system, camera interpolation, and portal instances. 137 were named, 60 with high confidence.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of 150 consecutive functions split cleanly into eight groups in address order: replay-camera helpers, a shared-memory media channel, particle sample baking, planes and ambient planes, corona light sprites, the nav and path system, camera interpolation, and portal instances. 137 were named, 60 with high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 unnamed game functions, with a confidence grade and one sentence of evidence each, working group-first rather than instruction by instruction.

What was found

Verified The batch held complete small subsystems: a plane class with constructor, destructor and damage, control and flight updaters; an ambient-plane manager that streams models and spawns and removes planes; a corona system from texture request through a 768-entry table to render; a nav system with config parsing, cell lookup, work queues and teardown; and portal constructors, destructors and bounds getters.

Verified Four inventory size fields were wrong: two functions listed as hundreds of bytes are tiny jump stubs, one overruns into its neighbour, and one range loop runs past its listed end. Sizes here cannot be trusted past the next function address.

Inferred Several existing symbol names are wrong and were not reused: a supposed script-array function is a plain memory copy by call shape, audio-system names in the nav region sit on code referencing nav data, and a pool constructor carries an animation name while building the portal pool.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the families other lanes already established for camera interpolation, particles and replay code. The next naming lane should diff twin functions against each other instead of reading both, and should treat any callee below the encryption boundary as unverified: several turn out to be allocator and lock stubs identifiable only by call pattern.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first (calls resolved against merged symbols, imports, string references, mnemonic profiles), then disassemble every short function fully and brief the large ones with entry plus call context. Confirm group membership by disassembling known callers rather than trusting callee names.

What was confusing or went wrong

The encrypted first megabyte makes every low-address callee name suspect, which was only obvious after decoding several and getting garbage. A probe script failed three times on data-section reads that return no bytes; string and constant reads from read-only data worked. Thirteen functions were left unnamed: tiny setters, jump stubs, mode wrappers with unknown modes, and single-field getters whose meaning nothing revealed.

entry.title: Averaging helper reads an uninitialized stack word into its output
entry.summary: Verified One of this batch's task functions writes four output words, and the fourth is whatever happened to be on the stack: the function never stores to that slot. Its in-batch caller never reads the word back, so the garbage goes nowhere there.
entry.content:
Verified One of this batch's task functions writes four output words, and the fourth is whatever happened to be on the stack: the function never stores to that slot. Its in-batch caller never reads the word back, so the garbage goes nowhere there.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the checker, covering the documented edge cases.

What was found

Verified All four rewrites passed twelve hundred trials each with bit-exact float comparison and a caught wrong version per function. While mapping the averaging helper's outputs, its fourth output word traced back to a stack slot the function reserves but never writes: on every call the word leaks one word of whatever the stack held below the call frame.

Verified The proof contract pins uninitialized stack to zero, so both sides read zero there deterministically; the rewrite writes the zero explicitly and the narrowing is recorded. The word is a genuine output of the original, just not a meaningful one.

Inferred The neighbouring selector function calls this helper with scratch memory and checks only the success flag, so the garbage word is harmless on that path. Whether any other caller reads it is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

Record stack-fill narrowing explicitly whenever a rewrite replaces an uninitialized read with the filled value, and check the in-batch callers for whether the word is consumed. Later lanes mapping other outputs of this helper family should assume trailing words may be uninitialized until traced.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the averaging helper and list every store to its frame: three float slots and the count get stored, the slot later copied to the fourth output word does not. Run the checker contract with a defined stack fill and confirm the output word equals the fill on both sides.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two mapping mistakes cost the most time. First, two registers were assumed to hold the same argument where the push count showed they hold different ones; the probe faulted on nearly every trial until the arithmetic was redone. Second, one float store was attributed to the wrong frame slot because a push sits between the address computation and the store; the snapshot comparison caught it on the first probe.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: zone population, montage music UI, replay records
entry.summary: A batch of 150 consecutive functions split into four clear groups: a zone population density system, the montage video editor music container UI, replay audio event records, and the replay camera. 85 got names and 65 were left unnamed, almost all of them one-instruction shared UI accessors whose field purpose no tracked source defines.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 consecutive functions split into four clear groups: a zone population density system, the montage video editor music container UI, replay audio event records, and the replay camera. 85 got names and 65 were left unnamed, almost all of them one-instruction shared UI accessors whose field purpose no tracked source defines.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium, or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and leaving the name empty where the purpose cannot be told.

What was found

Verified The population system reads six parallel per-zone density tables through one shared index shape, and the counts it computes feed cop-spawn checks and slot clamps.

Verified The montage clip-tag and music-track lists are stored as obfuscated comma-separated strings that a shared pipeline decodes and tokenizes before use.

Verified Replay audio events come in writer and applier pairs keyed by a one-byte record tag: writers serialize timestamp, entity, and payload from emit handlers, while appliers resolve the handle and replay the event during record processing. Nine tags were mapped.

Verified The frame container classes share one slot-list protocol (array pointer, count, add, remove), and the class-hash virtual slot is used for runtime type checks between frame classes.

Verified Two batch entries are alternate entries or tail continuations of neighbours rather than independent functions: one frontend update reached two bytes into another, and one zone update that jumps into the next function.

What was decided or recommended

One-instruction accessors shared across dozens of UI classes were left unnamed at low confidence, since their mechanical behavior is clear but no source defines what the fields control. The next naming lane covering UI accessors should check whether any caller or override has since given those fields meaning before renaming them. The two entry-sharing pairs should probably be merged in the function queue.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch entry, and cross-reference string references, import calls, caller names from merged lane symbols, class slot descriptions, and verified rewrite doc comments. A global-reference scan over the whole image finds the consumers of shared state that single-function reads miss.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest known name below the call site repeatedly misfired inside long unnamed spans, blaming a UI slot stub or a script native stub for calls made by replay and camera code. Native-mapping names in the merged symbols turned out to be low-confidence lane guesses rather than native-table facts, so they were only trusted where the code shape agreed. The zone data filename could not be recovered because the path buffer lives in a load-state struct shared by many unrelated loaders.

entry.title: Two adjacent task-system functions never return
entry.summary: Verified Two of four neighbouring task-scheduling functions cannot return to their callers: every exit path pops one word fewer than the function pushed, so the return jumps to garbage instead of the caller. The other two functions in the batch rewrote and verified cleanly.
entry.content:
Verified Two of four neighbouring task-scheduling functions cannot return to their callers: every exit path pops one word fewer than the function pushed, so the return jumps to garbage instead of the caller. The other two functions in the batch rewrote and verified cleanly.

What was asked

Rewrite four adjacent task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, at one thousand trials or more per function.

What was found

  • Verified The first and fourth functions verified at 1200 passing trials each, with deliberately wrong versions caught in both cases.
  • Verified The second and third functions each push one stack word more than any of their exits pop. Counting pushes against pops on every path to a return shows all exits are short by exactly one word.
  • Verified The third function therefore resumes at whatever its caller's saved register held. Setting that register to two distinctive values in two probes produced faults at exactly those two addresses.
  • Verified The second function resumes at a frame-local value instead; a probe faulted at an unmapped garbage address that matches neither the return address nor the checker's blank-stack pattern.
  • Inferred Each broken function has a single caller that expects a normal return, so any in-game call reaching an exit either crashes or runs wild. Whether those call paths are live or dead is unknown.
  • Inferred A leftover register save plus a dead constant store just above it suggest a bad hand edit added the extra push without fixing the exits.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both functions were deferred as unverifiable: a rewrite can only match them by jumping to the same garbage, and the checker has no notion of a wild jump as correct behaviour. The jump target of the third function (an incoming register) is additionally unobservable to a rewrite.
  • Full retry kits were kept: analysis, contracts, rewrites and the fault verdicts, so a future lane can resume if wild-jump verification is ever defined.
  • Recommended for other lanes: balance-check every exit (pushes versus pops on each path to a return) before writing a contract. A push with no matching pop means the function never returns. A two-trial probe with a pinned register value confirms it in under a minute.

How to reproduce it

  1. Disassemble each function and count frame pushes against pops plus cleanup on every path that reaches a return.
  2. Run the original under the checker with the incoming register pinned to a distinctive value and a stubbed gate callee; read the fault address from the verdict.
  3. Repeat with a second distinctive value and confirm the fault address follows it.

What was confusing or went wrong

The stack pointer value after the return looked almost right (one word low), which first suggested a mere cleanup mismatch that the usual check switches could cover. It took a second look to see the popped return address itself was garbage, which is a different and fatal defect. One build also failed briefly because the previous probe's worker process still held the rewrite library; a retry seconds later worked, and no stray processes were left running.

entry.title: A whole family whose listed starts land inside the true functions
entry.summary: Five functions handed to one production lane turned out not to be functions at all: every listed start lands in the middle of a real function, and four of them land in the middle of an instruction. Underneath sits a family of seventeen identical dispatch thunks, sixteen of which were rewritten and verified.
entry.content:
Five functions handed to one production lane turned out not to be functions at all: every listed start lands in the middle of a real function, and four of them land in the middle of an instruction. Underneath sits a family of seventeen identical dispatch thunks, sixteen of which were rewritten and verified.

What was asked

Rewrite and verify five neighbouring functions in the pedestrian task subsystem, each a few hundred bytes, on the stock checker.

What was found

Verified None of the five listed addresses is a function entry. One points at an instruction boundary partway through a function, just after its setup call; the other four point into the middle of instructions. A scan of the program found no caller targeting any of the five, contradicting the inventory evidence attached to them.

Verified The true functions are seventeen consecutive instances of one template: a small setup call, a handler looked up once by a numeric id and then cached, optional pre and post observation hooks, the handler call with the arguments forwarded unchanged, and a use-count decrement. Members differ only in the id, the cache slot and the argument count (two to five).
